issues.issue: The preamble says the Agreement "shall be effective as hereinafter provided," but Section 17 fixes effectiveness "as of the date first above written," leaving no separate later-provided effective date. The two effectiveness statements cannot both be given independent work.

The $2,000 initial location fee obligation appears only in a WHEREAS recital and is never repeated in the operative sections, so a party can argue a recital cannot create the payment duty. Section 3(B)(2) states the location-fee duty operatively only for Subsequent Wells.

The recital says Farmee "may acquire an interest in the Farmout Lands described in Exhibit A and Exhibit B," while Section 2(D) limits what can be earned to 80/40-acre circles around producing wells. The recital's broader description may be argued to control or to color the operative earning provisions.

The clause makes all five exhibits "part of this Farmout Agreement" without any order of precedence, though Exhibit "D" (blank royalty rate, notice-based assignment right) and Exhibit "C" (duties imposed on an undefined "Operator") do not match Sections 4 and 15(D). Which text governs on conflict is unaddressed.

The definition treats a dry hole "plugged and abandoned" as a "completed well," which sits awkwardly with Section 3(D), where completion of a farmout well "as a well capable of production in paying quantities" is the earning trigger. Whether "completed" in Sections 3(A)(3), 3(D)(2) and 10(A) carries the defined meaning is unclear.

"Drilling unit" is defined by reference to "field rules or order of the applicable regulatory authority," which may not exist for these Kentucky tracts, leaving the term without content. The illustrative string "spacing unit, unit for production, or proration unit" does not fix the boundary.

The definition of "earning well" is circular: a well is an earning well if Farmee "is entitled to receive an Agreement and Assignment of Operating Rights," which is itself the thing the earning provisions determine. It gives no independent test for when a well earns.

"[C]apable of producing in paying quantities" is undefined and is the sole condition on which the 80-acre and 40-acre circles are earned. Whether a marginal or intermittently producing well satisfies it, and how overlapping circles or circles extending off the Farmout Lands are treated, is not addressed.

The catch-all "and other similar burdens on production" follows an enumeration of royalty, overriding royalty and production payment, raising an ejusdem generis question about what else counts. The defined term is also never used in the operative sections.

"Contract Depth" is defined as an interval ("from the surface of the earth down to a depth of four thousand feet") though Section 3(C) uses it as a single depth a well must be "drilled to." Whether reaching Contract Depth means reaching 4,000' or something less is left open.

"[T]he initial well drilled" does not say whether a substitute well commenced under Section 3(C) for a lost test well becomes the "test well." That matters for the Section 3(A)(2) and Section 16 August 31, 1996 deadlines.

The definition confines "shut-in well" to a well "that has previously produced," but Section 7(A) imposes the shut-in royalty on any capable well "whether or not such well has already produced." The two cannot both be given effect on which wells are shut-in wells.

"[C]ommercial quantities" is used here while the rest of the Agreement (Sections 2(D), 3(B), 3(D), 5(A)) uses "paying quantities," and neither term is defined. Whether the two standards differ is unresolved.

A "subsequent well" is defined as one drilled after the "drilling and completion" of the test well, yet Section 3(B) allows Subsequent Wells once the test well is "plugged and abandoned" rather than completed. The definition and the operative trigger do not match.

"Unearned Farmout Land" turns on Operating Rights not having been "earned," but Section 2(D) makes earning depend on a well being capable of production in paying quantities, so acreage inside a circle around a marginal well is of indeterminate status. Section 5(B)'s termination as to Unearned Farmout Lands turns on that status.

"Payout" uses "gross proceeds attributable to the sale or production from a well" without saying whose proceeds, whether burdens and severance taxes come out first, and it counts only drilling, completing and equipping costs, not operating costs. Because Section 4 escalations turn on Payout, the measure is materially indeterminate.

The test well may be located "on a drilling unit that includes all or a portion of Farmout Lands," i.e. off the Farmout Lands entirely, while Section 2(D) grants operating rights only in circles lying within the Farmout Lands. What is earned by an off-tract well is left unresolved.

This deadline requires only that Farmee "commence the actual drilling" by August 31, 1996, whereas Section 16 conditions the Right of First Refusal on Farmee having "drill[ed] and complete[d] the test well on or before August 31, 1996." The same date is given two different performance standards.

"[R]eaching total depth" is undefined and is not tied to the defined "Contract Depth," so the start of the forty-five-day period depends on Farmee's unilateral decision to stop drilling. The clause also does not say what completion consists of.

This paragraph says Farmee "shall have the option" to drill Subsequent Wells, while Section 3(B)(3) says Farmee "must commence the actual drilling of two (2) Subsequent Wells" by December 31, 1996. Whether the subsequent drilling is optional or obligatory cannot be answered from the two together.

The fee is to be paid "[p]rior to the commencement of each Subsequent Well" but Farmee "will promptly pay" it, and the two timing standards differ. It also does not say whether wells located off the Farmout Lands on a unit trigger the fee more than once.

"[A]t Farmee's further option, it shall continuously develop" is internally contradictory — "option" and "shall" in the same sentence — so whether the two-wells-per-calendar-year continuous development program is a commitment or an election is unresolved. "[F]ully developed" is also given no measure.

Section 13(A) treats failure under Section 3(B)(3) as a "failure to meet the drilling commitments" that terminates the Agreement, which cannot be squared with this clause casting the same drilling as Farmee's option. Termination for declining an option is incoherent.

The forty-five-day clock again runs from "reaching total depth in each well," a point the Agreement nowhere defines or ties to Contract Depth. Whether "each well" includes substitute wells drilled under Section 3(C) is also unstated.

"[L]ost for any reason" and "mechanical difficulty or formation or condition which would render further drilling impractical or impossible" set no objective standard and leave the excuse largely to Farmee's judgment. "[I]mpractical" in particular has no boundary.

The assignment obligation runs from the date "Farmor is satisfied" that Farmee has complied with all its obligations, an open-ended subjective condition with no standard, deadline, or duty to review. Farmor's dissatisfaction could defer the assignment indefinitely.

This forfeiture measures the sixty days from when "a well has been completed as a well capable of production in paying quantities," while Section 3(D)(1) measures Farmor's delivery obligation from when Farmor "is satisfied" of compliance. The two clocks do not correspond, and the forfeiture consequence turns on which controls.

Depths earned are measured as "100' below the total depth drilled, not to exceed 4,000'," while the Exhibit "D" form of assignment reserves everything below a named (blank) formation. The depth actually conveyed by the assignment therefore depends on which measure governs.

This paragraph terminates the Agreement automatically, without notice or cure, for failure to "commence, continue drilling or complete any well," though Section 3(B)(3) casts continuous development as being "at Farmee's further option." Automatic forfeiture for declining an option cannot be squared with that.

The takeover right is made "subject to the terms of Section 6 below," but Section 6 by its own words applies only where "Farmor elects to take over a well under the terms and conditions of Section 5," not on a Farmee default. The cross-reference leaves the mechanics and the salvage-reimbursement duty of a default takeover unresolved.

Farmor "reserves the right to escalate" the overriding royalty on Payout, with no mechanism, notice requirement, deadline, or statement of whether escalation is automatic or elective. Whether the escalation ever takes effect, and from when, cannot be determined from the words used.

The proportionate-reduction sentence is garbled — "if Farmor's interest in the acreage is less than one hundred percent (100%) or the working interest" — so the trigger for reduction cannot be read as written. "[G]ross proceeds ... without deductions of any kind" likewise does not say whether post-production costs may be netted.

The notice duty is triggered when a well "ceases production," with no duration or materiality qualifier, so any temporary cessation arguably requires an immediate plugging notice. That sits uneasily with Section 7(A), which contemplates capable wells being shut in for forty-five days or longer against payment of a shut-in royalty.

This clause terminates the Agreement if Farmee plugs a well "without written notification and Farmor's approval," but Section 5(A) requires only notice and an election window, and expressly deems Farmor's silence an election not to take over. There is no approval requirement in 5(A) to breach.

The phrase "any Operating Rights Earned by Farmor and earned by Farmee" is self-contradictory as written, since Operating Rights Earned is defined in Section 2(D) as rights earned by Farmee alone. What Farmee must assign on a takeover therefore cannot be determined from the text.

The shut-in royalty is imposed on any capable well "whether or not such well has already produced," which contradicts the Section 2(H) definition of "shut-in well" as one that "has previously produced." Which wells owe the $500 depends on which prevails.

"Wheri [When] possible" qualifies the ten-day advance shut-in notice with no standard for when notice is impossible, making the obligation effectively unenforceable. Nothing states the consequence of failing to give it.

The indemnity covers claims "arising out of, in connection with, or resulting from the operations, actions or omissions of Farmee" without any express reference to Farmor's own negligence or fault. Whether it reaches losses caused in part by Farmor is not resolved by the words used.

"[F]ree and clear from all liens" is absolute, with no carve-out for statutory operator's or mechanic's liens being contested in good faith or for liens arising from Farmor's own acts. What counts as keeping the lands free of "all" liens is not bounded.

"Farmor does not warrant title, either express or implied" disclaims only title warranties and says nothing about Farmor's capacity to grant the operating rights or about the leases' validity, which Section 12 and Exhibit "D" assume. The scope of what is disclaimed is left open.

Well data and notices are to be given "as provided in Exhibit C," but Exhibit "C" imposes its duties on "Operator" and gives access to "EREX," neither of which is a defined party to this Agreement. Whether Farmee owes those duties, and to whom, depends on reconciling the two.

Confidentiality runs "for a period of one (1) year after any such well is completed," and "completed" is defined in Section 2(A) to include a dry hole plugged and abandoned. The start of the confidentiality period thus varies with which sense of completion is used.

The clause says notices "shall be given as follows" and then supplies only addresses, saying nothing about permitted method (mail, fax, hand) or when a notice is deemed received. The thirty-day cure and election periods elsewhere in the Agreement all depend on that.

The insurance covenant names three coverages but states no policy limits, deductibles, carrier ratings, or period of coverage, so what suffices is indeterminate. "[A]cquire and/or maintain" also does not say by when.

The heading "MODIFICATIONS AND AMENDMENTS" does not match the text, which is an after-acquired-interest clause about Farmor's retained interests attaching to renewals and amendments of leases. The Agreement contains no amendment procedure at all, so a reader looking here is misdirected.

Section 13(A) states the Agreement terminates "pursuant to Sections 3(A)(2), 3(B)(3), 3(F), and/or 5(B)," but 3(A)(2) and 3(B)(3) contain only deadlines and no termination language, and the list omits the forfeiture in 3(D)(2). The cross-references cannot be squared with the sections cited.

The clause first says the audit right arises "[u]pon written notice" and then that it "may be exercised by notifying Farmee in writing thirty (30) days prior," giving two different notice requirements. It also fixes no limitation period, frequency limit, or records-retention duty.

"[A]ll obligations, burdens and requirements set forth hereunder or otherwise associated with the lands covered hereby" is an unbounded catch-all sweeping in duties found nowhere in the instrument. What obligations are "otherwise associated with the lands" has no stated limit.

"[A]s nearly as possible to its original condition" states no measurable restoration standard and no time for performance. The duty to obtain permission "from both the surface owner and tenant" also does not address tracts with no tenant or with multiple owners.

Access "at all times" for Farmor's employees "at the sole risk of Farmor" sits against Section 8(A), which places operations under the "exclusive control of Farmee" and makes Farmee indemnify Farmor for all claims arising from operations. Who bears loss when a Farmor representative is injured on the derrick floor is contestable.

Section 15(D) bars any assignment by Farmee without Farmor's prior written consent, while the Exhibit "D" form of assignment (made part of the Agreement by Section 1) permits Assignee to assign on written notice so long as it retains a 25% working interest. The two assignment regimes cannot both govern a transfer of earned rights.

The Annual Report is due "on January 31st of each year" covering "production during the preceding year," without identifying the first or last report year or whether "year" means calendar year. No consequence is stated for failure, though Section 3(F)(2) treats any default as terminable.

The clause is labelled a "Right of First Refusal" but operates as a preferential right exercisable on the terms of this Agreement rather than on the terms of any third-party offer, and Farmor need only offer "to farmout same" without stating the terms offered. What Farmee is entitled to receive on election is therefore indeterminate.

The condition here is that Farmee "drills and completes the test well on or before August 31, 1996," whereas Section 3(A)(2) requires only that drilling be commenced by that date and Section 3(A)(3) allows forty-five days after total depth to complete. The two cannot both state the test-well standard for that date.

The covenants "shall run in favor of and be binding upon the parties hereto, their successors and assigns, and shall run with said Farmout Lands," which is hard to square with Section 15(D)'s bar on any assignment by Farmee without Farmor's written consent. Whether an unconsented successor takes subject to and with the benefit of the Agreement is left open.
